extracted.intended_audience: authors planning or writing long epic fantasy (multi-volume) series
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, pacing, and managing narrative complexity when writing a multi-volume (more-than-a-trilogy) epic fantasy series, with emphasis on structure, points-of-view, subplots, and long-term discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick a structure, and stick to it.
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide on a structure (mostly a set number of books) before you begin and use it to guide pacing and narrative decisions: "Pick a structure, and stick to it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the planned length/number-of-books to judge when to introduce or resolve subplots, whether to add characters or scenes, and when to ruthlessly edit. Examples: Rowling planned seven books and kept each book to roughly an academic-year unit; Erickson reportedly set out for ten and delivered. Anti-patterns: expanding a series ad hoc (ASoIaF moving from trilogy to possibly eight books) can cause pacing and coherence problems. Notes: discipline may require cutting satisfying material for the sake of overall shape; hammer in "pegs" (fixed events) to anchor the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control your points of view.
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit and manage POV characters carefully; add a new POV only if necessary and justifiable: "Every time you go to add a new point of view character, ask yourself whether it’s necessary, and then ask yourself again."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether information could be obtained by existing protagonists or shown rather than told through a new head. Anti-patterns: introducing minor POVs to "tell" the reader what villains are doing (example: Jaichim Carridin scene spent mostly on thinking), single-chapter/one-scene POV characters (Wheel of Time had many characters with only one POV scene). Consider counts and pacing impacts: many POVs fragment wordcount and slow forward momentum unless viewpoints overlap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of viewpoint characters relative to pacing.
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of the arithmetic of splitting wordcount across POVs: the more characters with POV, the less forward movement each gets per book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overlapping interactions between viewpoint characters to maintain momentum when multiple POVs are required. Example: Scalzi’s point — 120K with one POV vs split across many characters; fragmentation reduces perceived progress. Anti-pattern: dozens of POVs with most getting only a chapter or two per book (ASoIaF/Wheel of Time issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control your subplots.
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep subplot quantity and length in check so they don't stretch the series beyond its structure: "Control your subplots."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two failure modes: (1) show X happening far earlier than it affects the plot and add POV to do so; (2) give a character POV and then invent ongoing work just to justify that POV. If a subplot threatens to overrun the plan, either accomplish its elements more efficiently or cut it. Anti-patterns: making up subplot to keep a character busy (example: the 'Shaido Plot From Hell' created to give Perrin something to do). Option: give characters a deliberate "sabbatical" when their arc is in a consolidation phase, but choose points where something has wrapped up, not just begun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize and bring characters together periodically.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting major characters remain separated for too long; periodically reunite or overlap them so arcs remain connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizing interactions mitigates subplot fragmentation and keeps multiple plotlines tied to the central narrative. Anti-patterns: long stretches (multiple books) without main characters meeting (Wheel of Time example: Rand, Perrin, Mat, Egwene, Elayne separated for many books; ASoIaF fragmentation). Use reunions or overlapping scenes to ensure each POV progresses the central story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show less routine "math" as the series progresses.
rubrics_metrics.description: As readers become familiar with characters' competencies and routine tasks, you can stop showing every mechanical step: "The further you go, the less you have to show your math."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve detailed step-by-step scenes for genuinely novel challenges or character development. Anti-patterns: repeating mundane logistical scenes (camp logistics, throne-arranging) and excessive repetition of established mechanics (example: repeated explanations of Min’s visions). If readers may have forgotten, minimal recap/exposition is acceptable, but keep it tight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid "lazy" telling through minor POVs; force protagonists to protag more.
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use new POVs as the easiest route to convey necessary information; instead arrange for protagonists to discover or witness important facts whenever possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling via a villain’s interiority that mostly contains exposition is lazy and weakens the story. Encouraging protagonists to find things out makes them more active and improves narrative engagement. Example: Jaichim Carridin scene — mostly thinking rather than acting; could have been handled by protagonists learning the info.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be disciplined with editing and planning checks.
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent check-ins with your plan and "ruthless editing" are required to keep a long series under control and to "murder some very beloved darlings."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly evaluate whether scenes, POVs, or subplots serve the planned structure and theme; remove those that jeopardize the overall arc even if personally cherished. Notes: planning frameworks (thematic or structural) are often arbitrary but useful; discipline may feel constraining yet prevents sprawl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use thematic focus as a metric for additions.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use theme to judge whether new subplots or digressions dilute or overemphasize the central message: "Are you diluting your thematic message by adding in all these other subplots?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether a subplot supports, enriches, or distracts from the core thematic lines. Anti-patterns: adding many variations on a motif until the message becomes redundant; conversely, scattering theme through too many unrelated subplots dilutes impact. A central thematic line remains vital even in multi-volume works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of commercial/externally driven expansion risks.
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that external incentives (publisher pressure, profit) can encourage stretching a series beyond its artistic plan, which may harm story shape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh commercial temptations against craft: expanding because a series sells may increase revenue but can erode narrative discipline. The essay notes rumors Jordan was asked to stretch the Wheel of Time; the author recommends preferring disciplined storytelling over opportunistic expansion to keep readers' affection.
